patient_summary:
Hello there, I understand you're feeling quite weak and confused. Let's talk about what's happening and what you need to do next. 

You've been given some medicines to help your heart and blood pressure. You need to take them as prescribed:
- Coumadin 2mg every day
- Digoxin 0.25mg every day
- Prazosin 2mg every day

You should take these medicines exactly as your doctor tells you. If you miss a dose, let your nurse or doctor know right away.

You also need to watch out for any new symptoms. If you feel dizzy, weak, or have trouble moving your legs, you should call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away. 

Your doctors are trying to figure out why you're feeling this way. They think it might be because of a problem in your heart. They also found out you have a big tear in your aorta, which is a very serious condition. 

Your doctors are doing everything they can to help you. They're going to keep you in the hospital for a while to make sure you get better. 

Remember, if you feel any new or worsening symptoms, don't hesitate to call your doctor or go to the emergency room. Your health is very important, and your doctors are here to help you. 

Also, make sure you take your Coumadin 15mg every day as prescribed. This is a very important medicine to keep your blood pressure in check.
caregiver_checklist: Give Coumadin 15mg qd for 6 months under supervision.
Watch for signs of bleeding or bruising.
Call if INR is outside the normal range.
Watch for signs of heart failure or arrhythmia.
Call if heart rate or rhythm changes.
Watch for signs of hypotension or dizziness.
Call if blood pressure drops below 120/80.
Schedule annual physical exam and blood work.

source_text: CC:, BLE weakness.,HX:, This 82y/o RHM was referred to the Neurology service by the Neurosurgery service for evaluation of acute onset paraplegia. He was in his usual state of health until 5:30PM on 4/6/95, when he developed sudden "pressure-like" epigastric discomfort associated with bilateral lower extremity weakness, SOB, lightheadedness and diaphoresis. He knelt down to the floor and "went to sleep." The Emergency Medical Service was alert and arrived within minutes, at which time he was easily aroused though unable to move or feel his lower extremities. No associated upper extremity or bulbar dysfunction was noted. He was taken to a local hospital where an INR was found to be 9.1. He was given vitamin K 15mg, and transferred to UIHC to rule out spinal epidural hemorrhage. An MRI scan of the T-spine was obtained and the preliminary reading was "normal." The Neurology service was then asked to evaluate the patient.,MEDS:, Coumadin 2mg qd, Digoxin 0.25mg qd, Prazosin 2mg qd.,PMH:, 1)HTN. 2)A-Fib on coumadin. 3)Peripheral vascular disease:s/p left Femoral-popliteal bypass (8/94) and graft thrombosis-thrombolisis (9/94). 4)Adenocarcinoma of the prostate: s/p TURP (1992).,FHX: ,unremarkable.,SHX:, Farmer, Married, no Tobacco/ETOH/illicit drug use.,EXAM:, BP165/60 HR86 RR18 34.2C SAO2 98% on room air.,MS: A&O to person, place, time. In no acute distress. Lucid.,CN: unremarkable.,MOTOR: 5/5 strength in BUE. Flaccid paraplegia in BLE,Sensory: T6 sensory level to LT/PP, bilaterally. Decreased vibratory sense in BLE in a stocking distribution, distally.,Coord: Intact FNF and RAM in BUE. Unable to do HKS.,Station: no pronator drift.,Gait: not done.,Reflexes: 2/2 BUE, Absent in BLE, plantar responses were flexor, bilaterally.,Rectal: decreased rectal tone.,GEN EXAM: No carotid bruitts. Lungs: bibasilar crackles. CV: Irregular rate and rhythm with soft diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. Abdomen: flat, soft, non-tender without bruitt or pulsatile mass. Distal pulses were strong in all extremities.,COURSE:, Hgb 12.6, Hct 40%, WBC 11.7, Plt 154k, INR 7.6, PTT 50, CK 41, the GS was normal. EKG showed A-Fib at 75BPM with competing junctional pacemaker, essentially unchanged from 9/12/94.,It was suspected that the patient sustained an anterior-cervico-thoracic spinal cord infarction with resultant paraplegia and T6 sensory level. A CXR was done in the ER prior to admission. This revealed cardiomegaly and a widened mediastinum. He returned from the x-ray suite and suddenly became unresponsive and went into cardiopulmonary arrest. Resuscitative measures failed. Pericardiocentesis was unremarkable. Autopsy revealed a massive aortic dissection extending from the aortic root to the origin of the iliac arteries with extensive pericardial hematoma. The dissection was seen in retrospect on the MRI T-spine.
